clinicalPearls: A benign, non-neoplastic epithelial cyst arising from remnants of Rathke pouch, usually located between the anterior and posterior pituitary and intrasellar with or without suprasellar extension
Often an incidental imaging finding and asymptomatic
When symptomatic it can cause headache, visual disturbance from chiasmal compression and hypopituitarism, and diabetes insipidus may occur
Hyperprolactinaemia from a stalk effect can cause menstrual disturbance or galactorrhoea
MRI typically shows a non-enhancing cystic sellar lesion, and a non-enhancing intracystic nodule is a characteristic feature
It should be distinguished from a cystic pituitary adenoma and from craniopharyngioma, both of which it can mimic
Asymptomatic cysts are managed conservatively with surveillance, whereas symptomatic cysts may need transsphenoidal drainage or fenestration rather than complete excision
Recurrence can occur after drainage, so follow-up imaging is advisable
reference.pathophysiology: Rathke cleft cysts derive from the embryonic Rathke pouch, the ectodermal invagination that forms the anterior and intermediate pituitary. Persistence and expansion of the cleft between the pars anterior and pars nervosa produces a cyst lined by ciliated cuboidal or columnar epithelium, often with goblet cells, containing mucoid or serous fluid. Most remain small and clinically silent, but progressive fluid accumulation can enlarge the cyst to compress the normal pituitary, the stalk (raising prolactin by disinhibition) and the optic chiasm, and can disrupt antidiuretic hormone pathways. Rupture or inflammation of the cyst contents may provoke symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Craniopharyngioma, especially the cystic adamantinomatous form
additionalInvestigations: Pituitary MRI with contrast, showing a non-enhancing cyst and any intracystic nodule
Anterior pituitary hormone profile to detect hypopituitarism
Serum prolactin, which may be mildly elevated from a stalk effect
Assessment of posterior pituitary function with plasma and urine osmolality if diabetes insipidus is suspected
Formal visual field testing when there is suprasellar extension
Histology after drainage to confirm the epithelial lining and exclude craniopharyngioma
redFlags: Progressive visual field loss from chiasmal compression
Features suggesting cyst apoplexy or rupture with acute headache
Rapid enlargement or atypical imaging suggesting an alternative neoplasm
reference.prognosis: Generally excellent; incidental cysts often remain stable and symptomatic cysts usually improve after drainage or fenestration, although endocrine deficits may persist and cysts can recur, warranting follow-up imaging.
pitfalls: Attempting aggressive complete excision, which raises the risk of hypopituitarism and cerebrospinal fluid leak, when drainage or fenestration suffices
Misdiagnosing it as a cystic adenoma or craniopharyngioma
Missing associated hypopituitarism or diabetes insipidus before surgery
Failing to arrange surveillance imaging given the recurrence risk
references: Pituitary Society reviews on sellar cystic lesions
